title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
excerpt: Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging1–4, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an ‘add-on’ architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing various applications in synthetic biology and information storage. AutoDNA is an artificial intelligence (AI)-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments, realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework.

Data availability

The data supporting the findings of this study are available in the Article and its Supplementary Information. The sequencing data generated in the enzymatic DNA synthesis and DNA data storage experiments, together with the agent-related outputs, are available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20624108)53. Reference genome hg38 was downloaded from https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_000001405.40/. Further data are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request. Source data are provided with this paper.

Code availability

The code is available at GitHub (https://github.com/IPADS-X/AutoDNA). The version used in this study is available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20624108)53.

Extended Data Fig. 1 The automated hardware platform of AutoDNA.

a, The platform contains a series of workstations with distinct functionalities. b, A robotic arm (AUBO-i10) is responsible for transferring reagents among workstations.

Extended Data Fig. 2 Engineering design of the AutoDNA system for automated Nanopore sequencing.

a, Automated operation of Nanopore Mk1C is enabled by a high-precision robotic arm guided by a dual-camera machine vision system. b, The original cover of the sequencing flow cell is replaced with a custom-designed one engineered for robotic gripping. c, The robotic arm’s gripper can be directly used for the installation and removal of the custom cover. d, A high-precision camera (GTS-8016) is used to precisely locate the flow cell’s sampling port (~2 mm in diameter). e, An automated pipetting module (Keyto-SP16) dispenses liquid directly into the identified sampling port of the flow cell.

Extended Data Fig. 3 The user interface of AutoDNA.

The main panel displays the output of the current step, corresponding to the step highlighted in the Agent Workflow panel on the right.

Extended Data Fig. 4 Comparison of AutoDNA and manual NAT performance.

a,b, Representative real-time fluorescence curves from one of three independent experiments for the NAT assay executed by the AutoDNA (a) and by manual operation (b).

Extended Data Fig. 5 Normalized fluorescence kinetics in the strand-displacement assay for siRNA validation.

a, Commercially synthesized siRNA as the positive control and the corresponding no-template control (NTC). b, siRNA generated by AutoDNA and the corresponding NTC. c, An incorrect siRNA sequence as the negative control and the corresponding NTC. Solid lines represent mean values and shaded areas indicate s.d. from three independent experiments (n = 3 per curve).

Extended Data Fig. 6 PAGE analysis results during iterative optimizations.

Each iteration included four separately synthesized samples. Known-length oligonucleotides are indicated as size references. For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 1.

Extended Data Fig. 7 Timeline comparison of concurrent and sequential execution time.

Four enzymatic DNA synthesis protocols were executed concurrently after static code merging (Concurrent-1–4) or sequentially (Sequence). Coloured segments show the timing and duration of individual instrument operations, and arrows indicate protocol completion. The timeline shows a representative run from two independent experiments.

Source data

Extended Data Fig. 8 Real-time qPCR amplification curves for MUT, WT, and no-template control (NTC) samples using commercially synthesized primers.

a, Representative real-time qPCR amplification curves from one of four independent experiments. The MUT sample shows an earlier and stronger fluorescence increase compared with WT, while NTC remains flat throughout most of the amplification cycles, indicating good specificity and low background signal. b, Corresponding Cq values for MUT, WT and NTC. MUT exhibits the lowest Cq value, followed by WT, whereas NTC shows a substantially delayed signal with a Cq value close to the end of the tested cycle range. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. from four independent experiments (n = 4 per sample), with three technical replicates per sample in each independent experiment. Each data point represents the mean of the three technical replicates within one independent experiment.
